doc.title: Billy Bauer interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, March 22, 1998

chapter: Woody Herman and the war years
title: Earlier big bands, reading double stops, and tablature
summary: He had played with Wald, Abe Lyman and Carl Hoff, brushed up his reading for Hoff's book, and objects to tablature; he also mentions current students.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Reading music versus faking and playing by ear

blocks.x: So Woody Herman was the first big band that you had played with, of that size?

Well no, I was with Jerry Wald, I was with, Abe Lyman, I was with Carl Hoff from the west coast, he hired me. And at that time I had to go and brush up on my reading because in Carl Hoff’s band, the violin player was the arranger. There was only one violin, but he wrote double stops for the guitar and double stops for the violin so it would sort of sound like — that’s the book when I come in — and they couldn’t get any guitar player to read it. So I come closer to it, but I went down to Eddie Bell and told him gee, I’d better pick

up on my reading. So Eddie Bell says go and see Alan Reuss. But Alan was sick and he was going to go out to California. So I just went over two times with Alan. He says aah, keep doing what you’re doing, it’s all right. No, but that was lucky that I was taught how to read a little bit, on the banjo. See that’s what I try to tell these guys. This month, I think it’s May, April, May, I think it’s May, Jazz Guitar, there’s a magazine called just Jazz Guitar, they just sent me a proof of one of my solos I had recorded a long time ago. And I thought that was pretty crazy, if they’re copying it off the record. But now I realize they copied if off my music. But what they wanted to do, they put it in tablature. And that’s what I’m always against. I’m not against it, but if the guitar player reads that, he don’t read the music you know. It’s just like a block, like a cement block, that’s what you get, one of these, that kind of thing. What do you play?

I got a saxophone player now. What’s odd about him — well not only him, I’ve got a cellist, I’ve got a girl who plays all the woodwinds, but she wants to get in jazz. She calls it jazz but what she really wants to do, she wants to go, and I’ve got a cellist — because he does these weddings in the churches or in the synagogue or wherever. I don’t know. But he wants to get in, that he could do the dance part, and he realizes that he’s got the wrong kind of, you know. And so they come to me to get a little looser or whatever.
